name: Hammermen
text: A lock, a clock and a sword have surprisingly much in common: someone had to persuade metal to behave. Glasgow’s Hammermen gathered blacksmiths, goldsmiths, clockmakers and other metalworkers under one banner. Their engineering tradition continues today. The problems have grown more complicated; the satisfaction of making things work has not.
sourceTitle: Hammermen — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Tailors
text: The Tailors once tested newcomers by having them make garments in a locked room. This established two things: whether you could sew, and how you felt about deadlines with an actual door attached. They guarded Glasgow’s garment standards; today, their work also supports charity and education.
sourceTitle: Tailors — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Cordiners
text: Before a city can go anywhere, somebody must attend to its feet. The Cordiners brought together Glasgow’s shoemakers and other leatherworkers, supplying boots, jerkins and more. Their name recalls fine leather from Córdoba. A suitably grand word for people whose work met the pavement on your behalf.
sourceTitle: Cordiners — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Maltmen
text: Grain can become many useful things. The Maltmen took a particular interest in the brewing possibilities. Their guild watched over quality, apprentices and the workings of kilns and vats. Its leader is still called the Visitor: a title that sounds rather casual for someone inspecting your entire operation.
sourceTitle: Maltmen — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Weavers
text: A single thread is easily overlooked. Give it enough companions and a competent Weaver, and suddenly everyone has something to wear. Glasgow’s Weavers upheld standards in the weaving trade. They still encourage textile talent through educational awards: an excellent way of ensuring the next generation has something up its sleeve.
sourceTitle: Weavers — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Bakers
text: Civilisation is much easier to admire after breakfast. Glasgow’s Bakers supplied bread and, for centuries, ran their own flour mills beside the Kelvin. This was a Craft that took the whole business seriously, from grain onwards. Today it supports people in need and students learning the baking trades.
sourceTitle: Bakers — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Skinners & Glovers
text: Skinning and glovemaking demanded skill: a glove is a surprisingly ambitious piece of clothing, given how many directions fingers insist on going. Glasgow’s Skinners set standards for workmanship and trained apprentices. They also organised help for struggling members and their families. Keeping people covered was more than a trade.
sourceTitle: Skinners & Glovers — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Wrights
text: The Wrights are carpenters: people who look at timber and see something rather more useful than a tree lying down. Their Craft helped shape Glasgow’s built world. Today, their awards encourage young woodworkers, recognising skill, learning and finishing on time. Even a beautifully made thing must eventually be finished.
sourceTitle: Wrights — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Coopers
text: A barrel is a collection of pieces of wood that have agreed, under expert supervision, to hold a drink. Coopers supplied that expertise. Glasgow’s Craft demanded careful workmanship and long apprenticeships; it still supports coopering skills today. A small gap in the knowledge could mean a large puddle on the floor.
sourceTitle: Coopers — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Fleshers
text: The Fleshers were Glasgow’s butchers, overseeing the meat trade and the quality of what reached the table. Their rules even forbade leaving offal in the High Street. Some civic improvements need very little explanation. The Craft still maintains its industry links and a tradition of helping people in need.
sourceTitle: Fleshers — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Masons
text: Stone has very firm opinions about where it wishes to be. Masons supply the skill needed to turn it into buildings instead. Glasgow’s Craft remains connected with building and architecture, supporting apprentices and charitable work. It also keeps a Pear Eating evening. Even the most substantial traditions leave room for fruit.
sourceTitle: Masons — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Gardeners
text: Gardeners practise the patient art of asking living things to grow somewhere useful, preferably before the judging. Glasgow’s Craft supports horticultural students and apprentices, and celebrates the city’s floral displays through its Let Glasgow Flourish awards. A window box can qualify. Great civic ambition occasionally comes with drainage holes.
sourceTitle: Gardeners — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Barbers
text: A barber’s steady hand once had a considerably wider job description. Glasgow’s Barbers shared a history with surgeons, treating wounds and extracting teeth as well as shaving. Asking for a little off the top required some precision. The Craft’s connections with the medical and caring professions continue today.
sourceTitle: Barbers — The Trades House of Glasgow

name: Bonnetmakers & Dyers
text: The Bonnetmakers made hats, woollen socks and other comforting necessities. The Dyers brought colour, with standards intended to keep unreliable dyes from spoiling the reputation of Scottish goods. Together they covered quite a lot of a person. Today the Craft encourages young makers through prizes and support for education.
sourceTitle: Bonnetmakers & Dyers — The Trades House of Glasgow
